title: Cookies, a Dime and Kindness
text:
In 1972 the psychologists Alice Isen and Paula Levin asked whether a small bit of good fortune makes people kinder to strangers.

In their first study, students studying in a university library were either given a cookie by a passerby or not. Shortly afterward someone asked them to help with a study. The students who had received a cookie were more willing to help, and less willing to do something annoying to others.

The second study, the better known one, took place at public phone booths in shopping malls in San Francisco and Philadelphia. In those days, people often checked the coin return slot after a call. The researchers had planted a dime in the slot for some callers and left it empty for others. As each person left the booth, a young woman walking nearby dropped a folder of papers in their path. Of the 16 people who had found a dime, 14 stopped to help pick up the papers. Of the 25 who had found nothing, only one did.

A coin worth ten cents had nothing to do with the woman and her papers. But it seemed to lift people's mood for a moment, and a good mood made them notice and help a stranger.
lesson: Small pleasant surprises make people kinder. Brightening someone's day in a small way may set off kindness you will never see.
source: Isen, A. M., and Levin, P. F. (1972). Effect of feeling good on helping: Cookies and kindness. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 21(3), 384-388.
caveat: The samples were small and later attempts to repeat the phone booth study gave weaker or mixed results, though the link between good mood and helping is well supported.
